newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Colombian gov't, rebels take first peace steps.
newsitem.headline: Colombian gov't, rebels take first peace steps.

text.p: Colombian officials, meeting publicly on Thursday with a leftist rebel leader for the first time in six years, said the government would not demand a ceasefire as a precursor to launching formal peace talks.
"Dialogue must be opened in the middle of the war, without previous conditions," government peace commissioner Daniel Garcia told Reuters.

His rebel counterpart, Juan Antonio Rojas of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), did not comment on Garcia's position. But he said his forces were demanding conditions, including the disbanding of paramilitary groups, before talks could open.

The two men met in the presence of Medellin Archbishop Alberto Giralto in the Guatemalan town of Esquipulas 10 years to the day after Central American leaders met here in their first bid to end the bloody Cold War struggles of their countries in the 1980s.

The last time Colombian officials and the FARC guerrillas met publicly was in 1991 in Tlaxcala, Mexico. But talks to end one of Latin America's oldest conflicts broke down quickly when the two sides failed to negotiate a ceasefire.

The meeting revived hopes of a breakthrough in the stubbornly protracted conflict. But violence continued in Colombia this week, with another rebel group, the Marxist National Liberation Army, blowing up oil lines as part of a campaign to disrupt the country's infrastructure.
No representatives of the Colombian military were in town for the meeting.
Celebrating the Esquipulas peace anniversary, ex-leaders of five Central American countries also gathered here for a series of round table discussions on the experience of peace in their region.

Costa Rica's former President Oscar Arias, who won a Nobel peace prize for his efforts to broker peace in Nicaragua, El Salvador and Guatemala in the 1980s, said he had worked for three months to bring the Colombians together.
"The idea is to share our experiences in Central America, our successes and our failures," he said.
